1156.title: The fall from the horse
1156.hook: thrown and nearly killed, Montaigne found dying felt soft and dreamy, not terrible (Essays 2.6)
1156.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often return to this essay when they're afraid of dying: not as a promise, but as one man's careful report of how close he came and what it was like.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was we are patchwork: each piece of us plays its own game. Your line was patchwork.

An easy ride, not far from home, in a time of civil war. Montaigne is on a gentle horse that isn't very strong, with his men around him. One of them, a big, sturdy fellow on a powerful horse, wants to show off his nerve and get ahead of the others. He spurs hard, comes up behind at full speed, and crashes straight into his master. Man and horse go down. Montaigne lands far off, flat on his back, and doesn't move.
screen: `AN EASY RIDE NEAR HOME.` → `A RIDER AT FULL SPEED.` → `MONTAIGNE DOESN'T MOVE.`

segments.voice: First, the fall. Montaigne tells it himself in the essay Of Practice. He lies there stunned, bloody, his sword flung away, and his companions think he's dead. They carry him home with great trouble. On the way he starts to breathe and stir, and he throws up blood. Second, the surprise. What was it like inside? Not terror. His life seemed to be hanging on the edge of his lips, he says, and he closed his eyes as if to help push it out, and found a kind of pleasure in letting go, like drifting off to sleep. The feeling wasn't only free of distress; it had a sweetness in it. He wonders whether people we see thrashing near death are as far away inside as he was. Third, the return. Coming back was what hurt. Later, when his memory really returned, the whole fall came back at once, like a lightning strike, and only then did it feel like dying. Fourth, the point. Death, he says, is something we can't rehearse; when it comes, we're all beginners. But we can get close and look. This fall was the nearest he'd come, so he studied it. And he says plainly that this is his own study, not a lesson for anyone else. He doesn't promise anyone a soft ending. He reports what his was like: the moment itself was gentler than the coming back.

1157.title: Of books
1157.hook: he reads for pleasure and puts down any book that bores him (Essays 2.10)
1157.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often borrow his rule for their own shelves: read for honest pleasure or for what helps you live, and feel free to set aside what does neither.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the fall from the horse: the moment near death felt soft; the coming back was harder. Your line was softer than feared.

A bookmark that hasn't moved since spring. It sits in a book on the nightstand, a book you were told was important, and every night it gets a little heavier with guilt. Close by, maybe, another book you'd actually love to read is waiting its turn. Montaigne kept a library at the top of his tower, and in his essay Of Books, he tells us exactly what he does with the ones that bore him. He doesn't feel bad about it.
screen: `A BOOKMARK THAT HASN'T MOVED.` → `A LIBRARY IN A TOWER.` → `NO GUILT.`

segments.voice: First, why he reads. Montaigne says he looks for nothing in books except pleasure, honest amusement. Or, if he studies, he looks only for the learning that teaches him to know himself, and to live well and die well. That's his whole reading list: delight, or wisdom he can use. Second, no biting nails. When he hits something hard in a book, he doesn't bite his nails over it. He gives it a charge or two, and if it won't open, he leaves it; pushing harder only clouds his mind. And if a book bores him, he picks up another. Third, books in pieces. He's fond of Plutarch and Seneca, partly because their writing comes in separate pieces: you can start, stop, and come back, without a long commitment. And he confesses, a little daringly, that Cicero's long warm-ups, the definitions and divisions before the point, wear him out. He wants to get to the meat. Fourth, notes at the back. Montaigne's memory was bad, and he says so. So he wrote a short verdict at the end of a book, so he wouldn't pick it up later thinking it was new. That small habit matters. Reading for joy isn't careless reading. He wanted what he read to stay with him and change how he lived. Read for joy might mean closing the book you're dragging through, and opening one that wakes you up.

1158.title: Of cruelty
1158.hook: Montaigne hated cruelty, even to animals (Essays 2.11)
1158.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take Of Cruelty as a short, practical ethic: refuse needless pain, toward people first, and extend gentleness to animals and living things.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was of books: Montaigne reads for honest pleasure, or for what teaches him to live. Your line was read for joy.

A thin, high cry from the edge of a field: a hare, caught in the dogs' teeth. Montaigne calls the chase a violent pleasure. And in the very same breath, he says he can hardly bear to hear that cry. The same chase, the same dogs, and a man who can't quite enjoy the ending. He doesn't resolve the tension. He tells the truth about both, and that honesty sets the tone of his essay called Of Cruelty.
screen: `A CRY AT THE EDGE OF A FIELD.` → `THE CHASE, A VIOLENT PLEASURE.` → `HE COULDN'T BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: First, the vice he hates most. Among all the vices, Montaigne writes, he cruelly hates cruelty, by nature and by judgment, as the extreme of them all. Notice the joke: he hates it cruelly. The one harshness he allows himself is toward cruelty itself. Second, the small creatures. He can't watch a chicken's neck being wrung without discomfort. He can't stand the hare's cry. And he admits, a bit sheepishly, that his nature is so tender that when his dog offers him a game at the wrong moment, he can't say no. Third, the courts and the wars. Even in justice, he says, anything beyond plain execution seems to him pure cruelty. His own time is full of shocking examples, because of the lawlessness of the civil wars: people tormenting others for nothing more than the pleasure of watching. He saw it near home, and he names it. Fourth, the wider duty. There's a kind of respect, he says, a general duty of humanity, that ties us not only to animals, which have life and feeling, but even to trees and plants. We owe justice to people, and kindness and gentleness to other creatures that can receive it. He doesn't turn this into a rulebook. He doesn't tell anyone what to eat or whether to hunt. He draws one line, around unnecessary pain, and it starts small: the spider, the dog, the tone of voice.

1159.title: What do I know?
1159.hook: his motto was a question: what do I know? (Essays 2.12)
1159.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often use que sais-je as a pause before judging: a question that keeps the scales level until the weighing is done.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was of cruelty: Montaigne hated it above every vice, and owed gentleness even to animals. Your line was no cruelty.

Family crests. School mottoes carved over doorways. Slogans on coffee mugs. A motto is usually a statement, sometimes a boast, often an order: be brave, be first, never surrender. Montaigne picked a motto too, in French, que sais-je, and it isn't a statement at all. It ends with a question mark. In English: what do I know? And he gave it a picture to go with it.
screen: `MOTTOES GIVE ORDERS.` → `HIS ASKS A QUESTION.` → `QUE SAIS-JE?`

segments.voice: First, the question. The motto appears in his long essay called the Apology for Raymond Sebond, where he describes the ancient skeptics known as Pyrrhonists. Their way, he says, is to doubt, to inquire, and to hold back from settling on anything. Second, why a question. Language keeps tripping them up. Say I doubt, and you've claimed something: that you doubt. Say I know nothing, and you've claimed to know that. The idea is better held as a question, Montaigne says: what do I know? A question claims nothing. It just keeps looking. Third, the scales. He bears this question as a motto, he says, under the image of a balance: two pans hanging level, not tipped yet. That's the posture. Not I'm right. Not I know nothing. Let me weigh it. Fourth, faith and doubt. Montaigne was a Catholic, and the essay starts out as a defense of a theologian's book. Some readers see his doubt about human reason as a way of making room for faith, of saying our minds are too small to lord it over God. Other readers see a skeptic at heart. The essay is large enough for both readings, and this lesson doesn't pick one. Day to day, what do I know is a small pause before a big claim: about a coworker's motives, about how a story will end, about what that text message really meant.
screen: `A MOTTO THAT ASKS.` · `A QUESTION CLAIMS NOTHING.` · `THE SCALES HANG LEVEL.` · `ROOM FOR TWO READINGS.` · then, large: `WHAT DO I KNOW?`

segments.voice: Choose something everyday you feel sure of, not your deepest convictions, but something like what a coworker thinks of you or why a friend went quiet. Set it on one side of the scales and ask gently: what do I know, how did I come to think this, what might I be missing? Hold the scales level, without letting them tip, and breathe.

1160.title: The cat
1160.hook: when I play with my cat, who knows if she is playing with me? (Essays 2.12)
1160.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often remember the cat as a small lesson in humility: when we can't understand another creature, the gap may be ours as much as theirs.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was que sais-je: what do I know, Montaigne's motto, held like level scales. Your line was what do I know.

A piece of string dragged slowly across the floor. Under the chair, a cat goes flat, tail twitching. She wiggles, pounces, misses, and looks up at you as if to say that was on purpose. You're the one holding the string, so you're the one running the game. Aren't you? Montaigne had a cat, and somewhere in the same long essay as yesterday's motto, he stops to ask exactly that.
screen: `A STRING ACROSS THE FLOOR.` → `A POUNCE, A MISS.` → `WHO'S RUNNING THE GAME?`

segments.voice: First, the question. When I play with my cat, Montaigne writes, who knows whether she isn't amusing herself with me more than I am with her? It's a light line, and it flips the whole scene. Maybe you're the toy. Second, the silence between us. People and animals don't fully understand each other, he says, and we assume the failure is theirs. But why not ours as much as theirs? It's anybody's guess whose fault it is. By the same reasoning, he adds, they might think of us as the dumb animals. Third, the dog at the crossroads. He passes along a story from the ancient philosopher Chrysippus. A dog, following its master's trail, comes to a place where three roads meet. It sniffs one road. It sniffs a second. Then it runs down the third without sniffing at all, as if it had worked it out: not this one, not that one, so this. Montaigne doesn't wave the story away. He asks why we're so sure the dog wasn't thinking. Fourth, the point underneath. All of this sits in a long argument against human presumption. We're fragile, exposed creatures, he says, and at the same time the proudest, and we hand ourselves the top spot without much evidence. The cat is a gentle example: yesterday's question, what do I know, turned toward the creature on the rug. Who's playing whom is a good question for a pet, and not a bad one for a toddler, a teenager, or a boss.

1161.title: Of presumption
1161.hook: he describes his own faults with honesty and humor (Essays 2.17)
1161.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take Of Presumption as a model for honest self-description: naming faults plainly, neither boasting nor groveling, and keeping a sense of humor.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the cat: Montaigne wondering whether she was playing with him. Your line was who's playing whom.

I work too hard. I care too much. I'm a perfectionist. Ask someone to name their flaws, and sometimes this is what comes back: a boast wearing a disguise. Montaigne answers the question for real, in an essay he calls Of Presumption, and he doesn't disguise a thing. He goes through his faults the way you'd go through a junk drawer, holding each one up to the light, and some of them are funny.
screen: `I WORK TOO HARD.` → `A BOAST IN DISGUISE.` → `MONTAIGNE ANSWERS FOR REAL.`

segments.voice: First, what presumption is. Montaigne says it has two sides: thinking too highly of ourselves, and thinking too little of others. His own lean, he says, runs the other way: he tends to prize what others have and undervalue what's his. Second, the list. He's shorter than average, he says, and counts it a real drawback. His body was strong but clumsy at the skills a gentleman was supposed to have: dancing, tennis, wrestling, he was no good at them. His hands were so awkward that he couldn't read his own handwriting. He couldn't properly fold a letter, carve meat at the table, or saddle a horse. No excuses come attached. Third, the one thing he's proud of. Is there anything he does prize in himself? Yes: his judgment, his good sense. Then the joke lands on him. That's the one quality, he points out, that nobody in the world thinks they're short of. So even his pride is ordinary. Fourth, plainly, with a smile. This isn't self-hatred. He isn't groveling for reassurance, and he isn't fishing for compliments. He's accurate, and he's amused, describing his own faults the way he'd describe the weather. My faults, plainly, sounds like I'm bad with dates instead of I'm a terrible friend: true, specific, survivable, and maybe a little funny.

1162.title: The kidney stone
1162.hook: in constant pain from stones, he writes about bearing illness (Essays 2.37)
1162.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often turn to his pages on the stone as a picture of living with chronic pain: letting the body complain while keeping one's judgment steady.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was of presumption: Montaigne listing his own faults, plainly and with a grin. Your line was my faults, plainly.

What do you do with a pain that keeps coming back? Not one bad afternoon: a pain that arrives without warning, leaves, and returns when it pleases. Montaigne lived with one. He called it the stone, kidney stones, an illness he says he had dreaded long before it found him. In book two, chapter thirty-seven, the essay on how children resemble their fathers, he writes about living with it. Not as a saint, not as a doctor. As a patient, a little annoyed, a little curious, and still at his desk.
screen: `A PAIN THAT KEEPS COMING BACK.` → `HE CALLED IT THE STONE.` → `STILL AT HIS DESK.`

segments.voice: First, where it came from. His father had the stone too, Montaigne says, and he can't get over it. How could a tiny drop of seed carry the print of his father's illness, long before it ever showed? He doesn't pretend to know. It's the same shrug as what do I know, turned on his own body. Second, groan if you have to. He doesn't demand a brave face. If the body finds some relief in complaining, he writes, more or less, let it complain. What he guards is his judgment: that between the attacks he still thinks his own thoughts. The face can wince. The mind stays his. Third, the doctors. Much of the essay pokes fun at the medicine of his day: remedies that contradict each other, confident cures that don't cure. Hear that as a man of his time on the medicine of his time, not as advice about yours. His point is about being too sure, not about refusing help. Fourth, patience. He treats the stone almost like a stubborn houseguest: it comes, it goes, and he learns its habits. He even says the illness has been getting him used to the thought of dying, a little at a time. That isn't cheerful, but it's honest, and there's a steadiness in it. Patience with pain doesn't mean liking it. It means not adding a second fight, against the fact that it's there, on top of the first. Whatever the pain, let the body say ouch, and keep the mind your own.
screen: `FROM HIS FATHER, SOMEHOW.` · `GROAN IF YOU HAVE TO.` · `DOUBTING THE DOCTORS OF HIS DAY.` · `NO SECOND FIGHT.` · then, large: `PATIENT WITH PAIN.`
